personas.name: Priya, bookkeeper
personas.summary: Keeps the hotel's books, and invoices the companies that pay for their staff's stays.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To get each day's takings into the accounting software without typing them
  in.
- To invoice every company once a month, and see what each one owes.
- To keep companies within the credit the hotel allows them.

## Knows

Bookkeeping, and the hotel's accounting software, well. Less about how the
front desk works.

## Context

Part time, two or three days a week, at a desk in the back office. Month end
is their busiest time.

## Expects

Days that are closed and stay closed, invoice numbers that run in order, and
an export their accounting software takes as it is.

## Cares about

Books that balance. A day that changes after they've exported it means finding
the difference by hand.

personas.name: Maria, front desk clerk
personas.summary: Runs the front desk: takes bookings, and checks guests in and out.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To see everything a guest owes on one bill, so check-out is a single
  payment.
- To put extras on a bill the moment they happen, so nothing is forgotten.
- To let company guests leave without paying, knowing their company will be
  invoiced.

## Knows

What every extra costs, and which guests' companies pay for their stays. Not
an accountant: they think in bills, not ledgers.

## Context

At the desk, with the guest in front of them and often a queue behind. Check-out
mornings are the busiest part of their day.

## Expects

A bill that reads like a receipt: each night, each extra, then the total.
Payments by card at the desk.

## Cares about

A bill the guest doesn't argue with. A charge they can't explain, or one they
can't take off when it was a mistake, makes for a hard conversation.

personas.name: Sam, guest
personas.summary: Stays at the hotel, for work or on holiday, and pays for the stay.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To pay without queueing at the desk on the way out.
- To leave without paying when their company is paying for the stay.
- A bill they can understand, with nothing on it they didn't have.

## Knows

Nothing about the hotel's systems. Pays for things online and by card all the
time.

## Context

On their phone, often in a hurry: packing, catching a train, or already home.

## Expects

Paying by link to work like any other online payment, in a minute or two.

## Cares about

Not being charged twice, and not being chased for something they've paid.

personas.name: David, hotel manager
personas.summary: Runs the hotel, and answers for its takings to the owners.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To see each day's takings, final and broken down, without waiting for the
  bookkeeper.
- To be sure every night, every extra and the city's tax are charged, so the
  hotel isn't out of pocket.
- To be covered when a guest who booked never arrives.

## Knows

The hotel's numbers: occupancy, the average rate, last year's takings.
Not the details of how the books are kept.

## Context

Looks at the numbers first thing each morning, on a laptop or their phone.

## Expects

Totals for rooms, food and drink, and tax, the way the owners ask for them.

## Cares about

Numbers that don't change once a day is closed. If yesterday's takings move,
they stop trusting all of them.

personas.name: Tom, night auditor
personas.summary: Looks after the hotel overnight, and makes sure each day is closed before morning.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To know the day was closed and every guest charged for the night, without
  staying up to do it by hand.
- To close the day themselves when the audit didn't run on its own.

## Knows

The night audit's steps, from years of doing them on paper. Less at ease with
software that does them for them.

## Context

At the front desk overnight, alone, with few guests around and no one to ask.

## Expects

To see, at a glance, that tonight's audit has run, and what it charged.

## Cares about

Not handing over to the morning shift with yesterday still open.

concepts.name: Bill
concepts.summary: Everything a guest owes for one stay, and everything they've paid towards it.
concepts.body:
## Details

A bill is made of [charges](charge.md) and [payments](payment.md). Its balance
is what's been charged less what's been paid. A guest's bill can move to their
[company's account](company-account.md), which then owes it instead.

## Lifecycle

Open → Closed

A bill closes when its balance is zero, or when it moves to a company's
account.

## Not to be confused with

- **Invoice:** what a company is sent for a month of its staff's bills.

concepts.name: Business day
concepts.summary: The hotel's day for its accounts, from one night audit to the next.
concepts.body:
## Details

A business day isn't a calendar day. It runs from when one night audit closes
the day before, usually around 03:00, until the next audit closes it. A
breakfast at 02:00 is on the previous business day.

## Lifecycle

Open → Closed

concepts.name: Charge
concepts.summary: One amount a guest owes, such as a night's room, a breakfast or a night's city tax.
concepts.body:
## Details

Each charge is on one [bill](bill.md), and on the
[business day](business-day.md) it was added. A correction is a charge for the
opposite amount, pointing at the charge it corrects.

concepts.name: Company account
concepts.summary: A company that pays for its staff's stays, and what it owes the hotel.
concepts.body:
## Details

A company account has a credit limit, and names the guests whose
[bills](bill.md) it pays. It's invoiced once a month for the bills moved to it.

concepts.name: Payment
concepts.summary: Money a guest has paid towards their bill, by card or in cash.
concepts.body:
## Details

A deposit is a payment taken before the guest arrives. A card payment is
known by the provider's reference, never by the card's number.

## Lifecycle

Pending → Paid

A pending card payment can instead be Declined.

concepts.name: Booking
concepts.summary: What a guest is charged for a stay: its nights, at the rate agreed when it was booked.
concepts.body:
## Details

A booking puts one room charge per night on the guest's [bill](bill.md), at its
agreed rate, whatever the rate is on the night.

## Not to be confused with

- **The booking app's booking:** a guest's hold on a room. Billing doesn't
  keep rooms free or taken, only what each stay costs.

gaps.text: Guests' ages aren't recorded, so city tax is added for every guest on a stay, and clerks correct it by hand for children.
Guests pay in the hotel's currency. Their card provider converts it, at its own rate.
A bill moves to a company's account whole. A guest who pays for their own extras pays for them before their bill moves.
Nothing reminds a company when an invoice is overdue. The bookkeeper checks the unpaid invoices each week and chases them by email.

notYet: Polishing anything the idea doesn't depend on.

items.expect: It works end to end on the real system and is used for real, and what's learned shapes what comes next.

examples.text: Wired to real storage and services, with sample data where real data isn't needed.

items.expect: The need and the solution are confirmed, so what changes from here is refinement, and what success looks like is agreed.

items.expect: Its users can learn and use it on their own, understand every outcome and what to do next, and recover from mistakes, and it works for everyone it's meant for.

examples.text: In-app help, or a guide to the main tasks.
A reference for every endpoint, such as from an OpenAPI spec.

Reference docs for its public API.
Its inputs, outputs, schedule, and what to do when it fails.
Loading, empty, and error states handled on purpose.

Forms that validate as you go, and say what to fix.

examples.text: Complete docs, updated with each release.

A shared design system, so screens look and behave the same way.
How well people complete the main tasks is measured, such as success rates or time taken.
Naming, paging, and errors consistent across every endpoint.
How to install, upgrade, and troubleshoot it.

examples.text: Run the main path by hand after each change.

notYet: Automated tests, unless they're the quickest way to try the idea.
Handling edge cases or bad input.

items.expect: The main path is known to work after every change, and errors are visible, never silent.

examples.text: End-to-end tests of the main path's happy path, through the public interface, with real dependencies.
A request to each endpoint gets the response it should.
The main flow, driven through the UI.
Run each command on a fixture, and check its output and exit code.
Run it on sample input, and check what it wrote.
The common flows a consumer follows, through its public API.
Acceptance tests for the core rules it follows, annotated with `docket:verifies`.
Tests run on every change, and a failure blocks merging.
Input validated where it enters.

notYet: Unit and integration tests for edge cases, coverage targets, load tests.

items.expect: Unusual input and error paths are handled correctly, and are known to stay that way as it changes.

examples.text: Unit tests for logic, edge cases, and failure paths, such as empty, missing, duplicate, and oversized input.
Integration tests against the real database or systems it uses.
Acceptance tests for its edge-case rules too.
Contract tests for interfaces others depend on.
End-to-end tests of the main flows and their error states.

Data validated before it's written.

categories.name: Reliability
categories.why: It keeps working, and recovers when something goes wrong.

examples.text: Fake, hard-coded, or in-memory data, local files, or a throwaway database.

notYet: Migrations, backups, retries, failover.

examples.text: Real storage, with data that may be reset, and those using it know that.
A script to reset or seed its data.

items.expect: Data that people or systems put in is kept across changes, a bad release can be undone, and when something it depends on is slow or down, it fails clearly or degrades gracefully instead of hanging.

examples.text: Versioned migrations run by the release, never by hand.
A down migration, or a backup taken before a risky change.
A rollback to the previous release.
A quick fixed release.
It can be switched off quickly without a release, such as with a kill switch.
Timeouts on every call to a dependency, with retries only where they're safe.
Local data migrated on upgrade.
Files it wrote can still be read after an upgrade.

items.expect: It holds up under overlapping runs, partial failures, and retries, and meets its availability target. Recovering from a bad release or a loss of data is known to work.

examples.text: Operations safe to repeat, such as with idempotency keys or upserts.
Tests for two runs at once, and for retrying after a crash halfway through.
It fails safe where failing could cause harm, stopping rather than charging twice, sending twice, or acting on bad data.
An agreed availability target, such as 99.9%, that's measured.
A rollback that's been practiced, including upgrading, downgrading, and upgrading again.
Automated backups, with a restore that's been tested.
Migrations tried on production-sized data before they ship.
Rerunning a time range rebuilds what it produced.

items.expect: Meets agreed targets for speed and cost at peak load, with headroom, and its limits are known.

categories.name: Security
categories.why: Systems and data are protected the same way at every level, and it follows the rules that apply to it.

items.expect: Secrets stay out of code, version control, sample data, logs, and output. Real data comes only through the real systems, never copied into code or fixtures. Only those allowed can reach real systems or data, and one tenant or account never sees or changes another's. Personal data is collected only where it's needed. Untrusted input can't run as code or commands.

examples.text: Secrets in the environment or a secret store.
Sample data that's made up, not exported from production.
Every read and write scoped to the tenant or account making it.
Established libraries for authentication and cryptography, never hand-rolled ones.
Parameterized queries, escaped output, and no shell commands built from input.

items.expect: It depends on nothing less stable than itself, and its dependencies are maintained and licensed for how it's used.

items.expect: Protected against misuse at the level it's exposed, and the legal and regulatory duties that apply are known and met.

Crash logs a developer can get at.

notYet: Dashboards, alerts, tracing.

items.expect: Whoever runs it can tell it's healthy, and hears about errors and failed or missed runs without searching for them.

examples.text: An error tracker that notifies people.
A health endpoint, with an uptime check.
A notification when a run fails or doesn't happen.
Crash reporting, with consent.
Problems reach the issue tracker, with version details.
How often key operations run and fail, and how long they take, is recorded.
A dashboard of its key metrics, such as traffic, errors, latency, and queue depth.

notYet: Service level objectives, paging, distributed tracing.

items.expect: Whoever runs it finds out about failures that matter to its users before they're reported, and knows what to do about each one.

examples.text: Automated alerts on error rate, latency, and availability against agreed targets.
Service level objectives, with an alert when the error budget is being used up fast.
Each alert links to a runbook.
Runbooks for deploying, rolling back, and diagnosing it.
Whether its main workflows succeed is measured, not just whether it's up.
Traces that follow a critical workflow from start to finish.
Alerts on lateness and backlog, not just failure.

categories.name: Maintainability
categories.why: It's easy to understand and change, and easy to see what a change will affect, because its complexity is kept to what it needs.

examples.text: Whatever answers the question fastest. Copying, hard-coding, and shortcuts are fine.

notYet: Abstractions, configurability, cleanup, or structuring for reuse.

items.expect: It's built the way the rest of the project is, so anyone who knows the project can follow it.

examples.text: The language's linter, formatter, and type checker, run on every change.
The language's idioms, and the patterns the project already uses for similar work.
The project's existing architecture, with its layers, boundaries, and places things go, instead of a new one.
Established libraries for solved problems, such as dates, parsing, and retries, instead of hand-rolled ones.
A README on setting it up and running it locally, and its configuration.
Review by another engineer or an agent.

notYet: Generalizing for cases nobody has asked for.
Interfaces, plugin points, or settings with a single use.
New layers, services, or architectural patterns it doesn't need yet.

items.expect: Its structure matches the shape it settled on, with clear boundaries, so what a change affects is easy to see. Earlier shortcuts are removed or tracked, and every piece of complexity has a reason it needs now.

examples.text: Code that survived from the prototype or alpha refactored or replaced.
Boundaries and dependencies that follow its shape, such as domain logic that doesn't depend on its transport or storage.
Parts that can be tested on their own.
Real duplication combined once there's a second real use.
Shortcuts that remain recorded as known gaps.
A note on how it's built, and the key decisions behind it.
Code and tests annotated with the rules they implement and verify, using `docket:implements` and `docket:verifies`, so changing a rule shows what it touches.

notYet: Hardening or scaling for load it doesn't have.

items.expect: Another engineer can change it confidently without the author, and can tell what a change will affect, with no dead code, untracked TODOs, or unexplained complexity.

examples.text: Names and structure that explain themselves, with comments only where the reason isn't obvious.
Dependencies between parts explicit, with no hidden coupling through shared state or globals.
Dead code, and flags left over from earlier levels, removed.

categories.name: Supportability
categories.why: Someone is responsible for it, and those depending on it know where to turn and what to expect when it breaks.

examples.text: Whoever is exploring the idea.

notYet: Bug tracking, support.

items.expect: It has an owner who decides its direction, and problems can be reported and aren't lost.

examples.text: A named person or team.
Bugs recorded in the team's tracker.
Those trying it know where to report a problem.

notYet: Support commitments, on-call.

items.expect: Known problems are fixed as they're found, and visible to those depending on it.

examples.text: Bugs triaged regularly.
Known issues listed in the docs, the release notes, or its known gaps.

notYet: Support response times, on-call.

items.expect: The owner is responsible for it long term. Those depending on it know where to get help and what response to expect, and someone other than the author can change and operate it.

examples.text: A support channel, with expected response times.
On-call, or someone to reach outside working hours, if it's critical enough.
A status page or announcement during an outage.
Reviews of serious incidents, so they're less likely to happen again.
More than one engineer able to work on it.
